name: Toys “R” Us
tierWhy: The U.S. chain liquidated all 735 of its stores in 2018; the name now belongs to the brand manager WHP Global, which puts it on shops inside Macy’s and on small, mostly temporary stores run by a partner.[^14][^16][^27]

dates.text: was taken private by Bain Capital, KKR and Vornado in a $6.6 billion buyout
filed for Chapter 11 protection in Richmond, Virginia
announced it would liquidate all 735 of its U.S. stores

title: Toys “R” Us (1957–2018): interest on its own buyout
description: Toys “R” Us invented the toy superstore. Interest on its $6.6 billion buyout took nearly all its operating earnings, and the last U.S. stores closed in 2018.

card.blurb: The store that invented the toy superstore was still selling $11.5 billion of toys a year when it failed. Nearly every dollar it earned from operations went to interest on its own buyout.

stat.label: interest in its last full year, on $460M of operating earnings

hero.dates: First Toys “R” Us store 1957. Chapter 11 on Sep 18, 2017. Last U.S. stores closed Jun 29, 2018.
hero.standfirst: The jingle said “I don’t wanna grow up.” The balance sheet did not give it the choice.
hero.deck: Toys “R” Us, the toy superstore chain, filed for bankruptcy in 2017 after recording $5.6 billion of interest expense over twelve fiscal years (derived), and it never went public again.[^2][^8][^9][^13] Charles Lazarus had built a supermarket for toys and, for a while, a quarter of the American toy market.[^31] In 2005 three investment firms bought the company for $6.6 billion and left it with the bill.[^3]
hero.artCaption: Original illustration in the spirit of the 1980s storefronts: rainbow stripes, a brown mansard roof and a long neck at the door. Not an official asset or the trademarked character.

findings.title: The stores made money. The capital structure spent it.
findings.text: In fiscal 2016 the company earned $460M from operations and paid $457M in interest. Over fiscal 2005–2016 interest expense totaled $5.6B (derived).[^1][^2][^8][^9]

findings.title: It had lost the price war before the buyout.
findings.text: Its share of U.S. toy sales fell from 25.4% in 1990 to 18.4% in 1997, and Walmart was the larger toy seller by 1999.[^31][^34]

findings.title: It rented its website to its future rival.
findings.text: From 2000 it paid Amazon $50M a year in base fees to run toysrus.com. A New Jersey judge ended the deal in 2006, and Amazon paid $51M to settle in 2009.[^32][^7]

findings.title: The exit never came.
findings.text: An $800M initial public offering, filed in May 2010 to repay debt, was withdrawn in March 2013. Fiscal 2013 ended with a $1.04B net loss.[^11][^12][^9]

findings.title: The name outlived the company.
findings.text: Lenders kept the trademarks in 2018. WHP Global took control in 2021 and in 2026 announced 120 U.S. stores, most of them small and on leases of up to twelve months.[^19][^23][^27]
